feed_description: A daily, no-fluff curated listening feed on AI mechanisms, models, agents, compute, business models, economics, enterprise adoption and regulation.

selections.episode_title: The rise and fall of agent civilizations
selections.why: Start here for the capability shift. A compact account of what happened when many coding agents were allowed to operate together, what emergent coordination looked like, where the system failed, and why multi-agent security now deserves to be treated as an engineering problem rather than science fiction.

selections.episode_title: Less about Models; More about Architecture
selections.why: The enterprise reality check. The useful question is increasingly not which model wins a benchmark, but how models are wrapped in architecture, context, tools, data, evaluation and controls. This is a good bridge from frontier capability to deployable systems.

selections.episode_title: Redefining Chip Architecture with Arm CEO Rene Haas
selections.why: The compute layer beneath the model race. Focus on how AI changes CPU and data-center architecture, Arm's move beyond pure IP licensing, supply-chain constraints, hyperscaler demand and where economic power may shift as inference scales.

selections.episode_title: Building AI Assurance Ecosystem with Bri Treece (PACT AI) and Dr. Rob Slone (UL Solutions)
selections.why: Regulation only matters if institutions can measure and verify systems. This gets concrete about assurance, continuous evaluation, standards, independent testing and the missing infrastructure between high-level AI rules and real-world enforcement.

selections.episode_title: Chasing Trillion-Dollar Companies, Founder Ambition, Token Budgets, and Regulatory Capture with Sarah & Elad
selections.why: Optional business/economics extension. Useful on outcome-based pricing, token and compute budgets, what could support trillion-dollar AI companies, and how regulation can become either a safety mechanism or a moat for incumbents.

editions.title: Foundation week: LLM mechanics, reasoning and the compute bottleneck

selections.why: Begin with the machinery. This is a compact, accessible explanation of next-token prediction, neural networks, attention, training, hallucination and retrieval-augmented generation. The goal is to build enough of a mental model that later discussions of architecture, reasoning and agents have something concrete to attach to.

selections.episode_title: AI Trends 2026: OpenClaw Agents, Reasoning LLMs, and More with Sebastian Raschka
selections.why: Now move from the basic transformer-era model to the modern stack. Sebastian Raschka explains why progress has shifted toward post-training, verifiable-reward reinforcement learning, inference-time reasoning and tool use; he also covers mixture-of-experts, attention efficiency, long context and where agentic systems still fail.

selections.episode_title: Memory chip mania isn’t going away, with Dan Kim
selections.why: Finish underneath the models. AI compute is not just about NVIDIA GPUs: memory bandwidth and high-bandwidth memory are becoming binding constraints. This recent FT discussion connects the technical bottleneck to supply, pricing, data-centre economics, China, industrial policy and the physical limits behind continued AI scaling.

editions.title: Daily 1: Architecture under the hood, then Astra from the builder

selections.episode_title: LLM Architecture in 2026: What You Need to Know with Sebastian Raschka
selections.why: Today’s foundation slot goes deeper under the hood. Raschka walks through how modern LLM architecture has evolved beyond a plain transformer: post-training, inference-time scaling, hybrid architectures, attention variants, KV-cache efficiency, reasoning systems and why implementation details matter. It is the right bridge from a basic mental model of LLMs to understanding why current frontier systems behave and cost the way they do.

selections.episode_title: Greg Brockman on Astra and the Future of OpenAI
selections.why: For the current slot, hear the builder’s account rather than a recap. OpenAI president Greg Brockman discusses what Astra changes about computer use and agents, what OpenAI learned from Operator, and how the company thinks about AI systems that carry out longer-running tasks. Treat the capability and scientific claims as OpenAI’s own framing, not independent validation; the value here is direct access to the product and research thesis behind the release.

editions.title: Daily 2: LLM vocabulary from the ground up, then stress-testing Astra

selections.episode_title: 303 - How LLMs Work - the 20 minute explainer
selections.why: Reset the foundation at the right level. This recent explainer builds a usable mental model from words to tokens, tokens to embeddings, and embeddings to inference, then introduces temperature and sampling. The aim is not to make you an ML engineer; it is to make the vocabulary in later episodes intelligible before we move on to transformers, training, reasoning and agents.

selections.episode_title: GPT-6 Astra: The System Card, Alignment and What Comes Next
selections.why: Yesterday you heard Astra from OpenAI president Greg Brockman. Today, Zvi Mowshowitz works through the actual Astra system card and external evaluations, focusing on the gap between strong capability/safety claims and what the evaluations establish. Pay particular attention to critical cyber capability, evaluation awareness, metagaming, alignment claims and reduced chain-of-thought monitorability. This is a critical reading rather than neutral reporting, so treat Zvi's conclusions as an interpretation too; the primary evidence is OpenAI's system card and the cited external evaluations.

editions.title: Daily 3: From embeddings to attention and agents, then who grades the models?

selections.episode_title: An Agent Is Just an LLM in a For-Loop
selections.why: Build directly on yesterday's Fragmented explainer without jumping back into architecture jargon. Maarten Grootendorst, co-author of Hands-On Large Language Models and An Illustrated Guide to AI Agents, revisits embeddings, adds attention as the next core mechanism, and then shows how an LLM becomes an agent when you put it in a loop with tools and memory. The useful mental progression is embeddings → attention → model call → loop → tools/memory, with practical discussion of where agents work and fail.

selections.episode_title: Who Grades the AI Models? | Ben Horowitz & Rayan Krishnan
selections.why: After two days of Astra claims and counterclaims, step back and learn how model claims are actually tested. Rayan Krishnan of independent evaluator Vals explains why public benchmarks saturate, why self-reported scores can mislead, how private and continuously changing evals work, and why agent evaluation is harder when tasks unfold over hours or days. Treat Vals' case for independent evaluation as an interested perspective too: the episode is hosted by a16z and is not itself an audit. Its value is the framework for asking what evidence should count before believing the next frontier-model claim.

editions.title: Daily 4: Attention without the jargon, then stress-testing the AI panic

selections.episode_title: Module 2: Inside the Transformer -The Math That Makes Attention Work
selections.why: This is the clean next lesson after tokens and embeddings. In about twelve minutes, Shay Dhar explains the transformer's attention mechanism in plain language, then introduces queries, keys and values, dot products, softmax and weighted sums without assuming ML fluency. It is unusually close to the concise, concept-by-concept teaching style that made Fragmented 303 work so well for you.

The frontier slot deliberately challenges the safety-heavy sequence of the past few days. Vox's Sean Rameswaram and Wired senior writer Maxwell Zeff examine the new calls from AI insiders to slow frontier development, including the real evidence from agent-control incidents, while also asking whether labs benefit reputationally and competitively from framing themselves as builders of uniquely dangerous technology. The point is not to dismiss the incidents or accept existential-risk claims: it is to separate observed failures from extrapolations about future catastrophe, and technical evidence from incentives and politics.

editions.title: Daily 5: What post-training actually does, then a reality check on recursive self-improvement

selections.why: Now that tokens, embeddings and attention have a mental model, move to the second major phase of building a useful LLM. AMD VP of AI Sharon Zhou starts with a plain-language definition of post-training and explains how a pretrained next-token predictor becomes an assistant that follows instructions, uses tools and reasons. The discussion introduces supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, in-context learning and RAG through their practical purpose rather than as a wall of acronyms.

selections.episode_title: Are We About to Lose Control of AI? | AI Reality Check
selections.why: Anthropic's new September disclosure says Claude now leads 26% of its AI R&D projects and participates in roughly 90%, reviving the recursive-self-improvement narrative. Cal Newport provides a useful skeptical audit of the underlying inference: faster AI-assisted coding and research workflows are evidence of automation, but not by themselves evidence that an AI can autonomously invent the algorithmic breakthroughs needed to build a substantially smarter successor. Use this as a counterweight, not a final verdict: his June analysis predates Anthropic's newest 26% figure, so today's stronger evidence raises the bar for the skeptical case without yet demonstrating a self-sustaining improvement loop.
